content: 1. Suvorexant is an orexin receptor antagonist approved by the FDA for the treatment of insomnia, specifically for difficulties with sleep onset and/or sleep maintenance. 2. Common adverse reactions to suvorexant include somnolence. 3. The recommended starting dose of suvorexant is 10 mg, taken no more than once per night, within 30 minutes of going to bed, and ensuring at least 7 hours remain before planned awakening. 4. If the 10 mg dose is well-tolerated but not effective, the dose may be increased, with a maximum recommended dose of 20 mg once daily. 5. 6. When suvorexant is combined with other central nervous system (CNS) depressants, dosage adjustments may be necessary due to potentially additive effects. 7. The recommended dose of suvorexant is 5 mg when used with moderate CYP3A inhibitors, and the dose should generally not exceed 10 mg in these patients. Suvorexant is not recommended for use with strong CYP3A inhibitors. 8. The time to effect of suvorexant may be delayed if taken with or soon after a meal. 9. Suvorexant is contraindicated in patients with narcolepsy. 10. Suvorexant, as a CNS depressant, can impair daytime wakefulness even when used as prescribed. Prescribers should monitor for somnolence and CNS depressant effects, which may persist for several days after discontinuation. 11. Suvorexant can impair driving skills and increase the risk of falling asleep while driving. Patients should be cautioned against next-day driving and other activities requiring full mental alertness, especially at higher doses. 12. Co-administration with other CNS depressants, such as benzodiazepines, opioids, tricyclic antidepressants, or alcohol, increases the risk of CNS depression. Patients should avoid alcohol while taking suvorexant. 13. Sleep disturbances may indicate an underlying physical or psychiatric disorder. Insomnia treatment should only be initiated after careful evaluation of the patient. 14. Cognitive and behavioral changes, such as amnesia, anxiety, hallucinations, and other neuropsychiatric symptoms, have been reported with hypnotics like suvorexant. Complex behaviors, such as sleep-driving and other activities performed while not fully awake, have also been reported. 15. Suvorexant use has been associated with a dose-dependent increase in suicidal ideation in clinical studies. Patients with suicidal ideation or new behavioral symptoms should be immediately evaluated. 16. The effects of suvorexant on respiratory function should be considered in patients with compromised respiratory function. Suvorexant has not been studied in patients with severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) or severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). 17. Sleep paralysis, hypnagogic/hypnopompic hallucinations, and cataplexy-like symptoms can occur with suvorexant use. These symptoms may include periods of leg weakness lasting seconds to minutes and may occur without an identifiable trigger. 18. In clinical trials, the most common adverse reaction reported with suvorexant was somnolence, occurring in 7% of patients treated with 15 mg or 20 mg doses, compared to 3% with placebo. 19. 20. Suvorexant is extensively bound to human plasma proteins (>99%) and is primarily metabolized by CYP3A, with a minor contribution from CYP2C19. 21. The primary route of elimination is through the feces, with approximately 66% of the radiolabeled dose recovered in the feces and 23% in the urine. 22. Suvorexant has a mean half-life of approximately 12 hours and reaches steady-state concentrations within 3 days of once-daily dosing. 23. However, dose adjustment based on gender is generally not needed. 24. Suvorexant should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. 25. Suvorexant and its metabolite were excreted in rat milk at levels higher than in maternal plasma. It is not known whether suvorexant is excreted in human milk, so caution should be exercised when administered to nursing women. 26. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established. 27. No dose adjustment is required in patients with renal impairment or mild to moderate hepatic impairment. However, suvorexant is not recommended in patients with severe hepatic impairment. 28. Suvorexant does not prolong the QTc interval to any clinically relevant extent. 29. Hemodialysis is not expected to contribute to the elimination of suvorexant due to its high protein binding. 30. Suvorexant exerts its therapeutic effect in insomnia by antagonizing orexin receptors, which are central promoters of wakefulness. Blocking the binding of wake-promoting neuropeptides orexin A and orexin B to their receptors suppresses wake drive.
